# Two cofactor families beyond the first-row boundary

Statement **R-025**. Written and checked on 21 November 2026 UTC by
GPT-6 Astra Pro, agent /root/rectangular_cases; effort setting not exposed.
Every assertion below concerns the displayed actual polynomial maps.
No historical novelty claim is made.

## 1. Explicit canonical image components at the critical degree

Let \(a\ge3\), put \(r=a-1\), \(b=r^2-1\), and \(H=r^2+1=b+2\).
Use the normalized canonical grid map
\[
h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b(\operatorname{Sym}^a V)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^b V).
\tag{Cof.1}
\]

For every **odd \(a\ge3\)**, equivalently every even \(r\ge2\), set
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{odd}\ a}
=(r^2+1,(r^2)^{r-2},r^2-2,r^2-r).
\tag{Cof.2}
\]
For every **even \(a\ge4\)**, equivalently every odd \(r\ge3\), set
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{even}\ a}
=((r^2+1)^r,r^2-2r-1).
\tag{Cof.3}
\]
Both are partitions of \(ab\). In every dimension at least their
number of rows,
\[
\boxed{
[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{im}h_{b,a}]
=[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^b V)]
=1
}
\tag{Cof.4}
\]
for the corresponding displayed \(\lambda\).

The proof supplies a highest vector in the dual target whose
last-slot common polarization is nonzero. The exact annihilator
inclusion (K.22) then proves (Cof.4). Thus this is a statement about
the canonical map on its unique target copy.

For example the families include
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
a&b&\lambda\\\hline
3&3&(5,2,2)\\
4&8&(10,10,10,2)\\
5&15&(17,16,16,14,12)\\
6&24&(26,26,26,26,26,14)\\
7&35&(37,36,36,36,36,34,30).
\end{array}
\tag{Cof.5}
\]
Their first row is \(r^2+1\). Apart from coincidences with previously
established full-map cases, these labels lie outside the two
component ranges \(\lambda_1\le r^2\) and
\(\lambda_2\le r(r-1)-1\) of R-022.

## 2. Two actual highest polynomials

First use \(n\ge3\) slots and \(n\) coordinate rows. Write
\[
X=(X_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n},\qquad
x_j=X_{1j},\qquad D=\det X.
\]
Let \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det X_{\widehat i,\widehat j}\) be the
cofactor matrix, and put
\[
y_j=C_{nj},\qquad z_j=C_{n-1,j},\qquad
\mathcal S(X)=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j z_j^2\prod_{i\ne j}y_i.
\tag{Cof.6}
\]

For every odd integer \(H\ge n+1\), define
\[
F_{n,H}=D^{H-n-2}\mathcal S(X).
\tag{Cof.7}
\]
The possible exponent \(-1\), occurring at \(H=n+1\), is
interpreted by the actual polynomial quotient
\(\mathcal S(X)/D\). This quotient is polynomial: on the dense
rank-\((n-1)\) locus of \(D=0\), all nonzero rows of the cofactor
matrix are proportional. In its fraction field \(z_j=c\,y_j\),
and
\[
\mathcal S=c^2\left(\prod_i y_i\right)\sum_jx_jy_j=0.
\]
The last equality is the cofactor identity
\(\sum_jX_{1j}C_{nj}=0\). The determinant hypersurface is integral
(the generic determinant is irreducible), so vanishing on this
dense open subset gives \(D\mid\mathcal S\) in the polynomial ring.
The same conclusion holds on charts where another cofactor row
is nonzero; one dense chart already proves the divisibility.

Each column of \(\mathcal S\) has degree \(n\). Thus (Cof.7)
has degree \(H-2\) in each slot, and its row weight is
\[
\lambda^F_{n,H}
=(H,(H-1)^{n-3},H-3,H-n).
\tag{Cof.8}
\]
This is a partition for \(n\ge3\) and \(H\ge n+1\).

Here is a direct highest-vector verification. Under a row
transvection \(X\mapsto (I+tE_{j,i})X\), \(i<j\), the cofactor
matrix changes by \(C\mapsto(I-tE_{i,j})C\), and \(D\) and the
first row stay fixed. The row \(y\) stays fixed. The only such
change affecting \(z\) is \(z\mapsto z-t y\). Under that change,
the difference of the two numerators in (Cof.6) is
\[
-2t\left(\prod_i y_i\right)\sum_jx_jz_j
+t^2\left(\prod_i y_i\right)\sum_jx_jy_j=0.
\tag{Cof.9}
\]
Both sums are zero cofactor identities, since \(n-1,n\ne1\).
Therefore \(F_{n,H}\) is a highest polynomial of weight (Cof.8).

A permutation of columns multiplies \(D\) by its sign and each
cofactor row by that sign while permuting its entries. Hence the
numerator in (Cof.6) has sign character to the power \(n+1\).
The total permutation character of (Cof.7) is
\(\operatorname{sgn}^{H-1}=1\). It consequently belongs to
\(\operatorname{Sym}^n(\operatorname{Sym}^{H-2}V)\).

The second polynomial, for every even \(H\ge2n\), is
\[
G_{n,H}=D^{H-2n}\prod_{j=1}^n y_j^2.
\tag{Cof.10}
\]
It is polynomial, symmetric in the slots, and highest by the
same transvection formulas. Its separate slot degree is \(H-2\),
and its row weight is
\[
\lambda^G_{n,H}=(H^{n-1},H-2n).
\tag{Cof.11}
\]

## 3. Exact multiplicity-one identification

We give the complement morphism that determines the multiplicities
of these highest vectors. For every partition \(\lambda\) fitting
in the \(n\times H\) rectangle, put
\[
\nu=(H-\lambda_n,\ldots,H-\lambda_1).
\]
Exterior multiplication of complementary columns gives the perfect
\(GL_n\)-equivariant pairing
\[
S_\lambda\mathbf Q^n\otimes S_\nu\mathbf Q^n
\longrightarrow(\det\mathbf Q^n)^H.
\tag{Cof.12}
\]
For precision, apply the wedge pairing on each column after
realizing both Schur modules by their column alternations and row
symmetrizations. On the complementary standard highest and lowest
tableaux it is a nonzero product of coordinate determinants.
Its map from either irreducible Schur factor to the dual of the
other, with determinant twist, is therefore nonzero and hence an
isomorphism. This proves perfectness and fixes the determinant
character.

Restrict (Cof.12) to content \(((H-2)^n)\) in the first factor and
content \((2^n)\) in the second. Diagonal weights add to \((H^n)\),
so these are perfectly paired weight spaces. Permutation matrices
act on the one-dimensional target by \(\operatorname{sgn}^H\).
Taking permutation invariants, and using the Cauchy decomposition
of matrix polynomials, gives the exact multiplicity equalities
\[
[S_\lambda:\operatorname{Sym}^n\operatorname{Sym}^{H-2}]
=
\begin{cases}
[S_\nu:\Lambda^n(\operatorname{Sym}^2)],&H\text{ odd},\\
[S_\nu:\operatorname{Sym}^n(\operatorname{Sym}^2)],&H\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\tag{Cof.13}
\]
The second step is the literal content-\((2^n)\) matrix-polynomial
space \((\operatorname{Sym}^2\mathbf Q^n)^{\otimes n}\).
Its sign-isotypic projector is \(n!^{-1}\sum_\sigma
\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma\), whose image is
\(\Lambda^n(\operatorname{Sym}^2\mathbf Q^n)\) under the usual
normalized alternating inclusion. Its invariant projector gives
the symmetric power. These are the actual maps in (Cof.13).

For (Cof.8), the complementary partition is
\[
\nu=(n,3,1^{n-3},0).
\]
Its weight space in \(\Lambda^n(\operatorname{Sym}^2\mathbf Q^n)\)
has dimension one. To see this, view a wedge basis as a set of
distinct quadratic monomials, with a loop counting twice toward a
vertex degree. No monomial uses the \(n\)-th variable. Degree \(n\)
at the first variable forces its loop and all \(n-2\) available
edges to the other variables. The one remaining quadratic must
be the loop at the second variable, which raises its degree from
one to three. Thus the unique wedge is
\[
e_1^2\wedge e_1e_2\wedge\cdots\wedge e_1e_{n-1}
\wedge e_2^2.
\tag{Cof.14}
\]
It is highest: replacing any higher-index variable by a
lower-index variable yields either zero or a repeated wedge
factor. Thus its irreducible type occurs once. For (Cof.11) the
complement is the row \((2n)\), whose unique highest vector in
\(\operatorname{Sym}^n(\operatorname{Sym}^2)\) is
\((e_1^2)^n\). This also occurs once. Equation (Cof.13) proves
multiplicity one for both displayed original types.

## 4. A concrete cofactor specialization

We specify matrices producing the needed positive coefficients.
Let the slot set be a disjoint union \(I\sqcup J\), with
\(|I|=s\), \(|J|=t\), \(s+t=n\), both sets nonempty. Choose a
reference slot \(q\in I\). There exists an explicit unimodular
\((n-1)\times(n-1)\) matrix \(A\) whose last row is the indicator
of \(J\), in the coordinates excluding \(q\): take one \(j_0\in J\),
keep every coordinate row except \(e_{j_0}\), and replace that row
by \(\sum_{j\in J}e_j\), putting it last.

For \(F\), also choose a nonempty singleton \(K=\{p\}\subset
I\setminus\{q\}\), and put the row \(e_p\) penultimate. The
remaining coordinate rows, in increasing order, precede these
last two rows. This explicitly gives the required unimodular
matrix in this case.

Let \(B_0\) have rows \(e_i-e_q\), for \(i\ne q\), in the same
coordinate order, and set
\[
B=A^{-T}B_0,\qquad
X=\begin{pmatrix}x_1&\cdots&x_n\\B\end{pmatrix},\qquad
X_I=\sum_{i\in I}x_i,\quad Y_J=\sum_{j\in J}x_j,\quad
S=X_I+Y_J.
\tag{Cof.15}
\]
All entries of \(B\) are integers. Direct solution of the equations
\(B_0v=(v_i-v_q)_{i\ne q}\) shows
\[
D=\eta S,\qquad
C_{\ell+1,i}=\eta\bigl(S A_{\ell,i}
                       -\sum_j A_{\ell,j}x_j\bigr),
\quad \eta\in\{1,-1\},
\tag{Cof.16}
\]
where the missing column \(A_{\ell,q}\) is zero. The scalar
\(\eta=D(1,0,\ldots,0)\) is the signed determinant of the displayed
constant row matrix and is a unit. Formula (Cof.16) is also the
identity \(C=D X^{-T}\); it fixes its scalar exactly.

The last two chosen rows give
\[
y_i/\eta=
\begin{cases}-Y_J&i\in I,\\X_I&i\in J,\end{cases}
\qquad
z_i/\eta=S\,1_{i=p}-x_p.
\tag{Cof.17}
\]
Writing \(Z=x_p\) and \(R=X_I-Z\), direct substitution into the
sum (Cof.6) gives
\[
\mathcal S(X)
=\eta^{n+1}(-1)^{s+1}S^2
 ZR\,X_I^{t-1}Y_J^{s-1}.
\tag{Cof.18}
\]
For example, divide temporarily by \(\prod y_i\): the two group
sums are
\[
-\frac{ZS^2+(X_I-2S)Z^2}{Y_J}
+\frac{Y_JZ^2}{X_I}
=-\frac{S^2Z(X_I-Z)}{X_IY_J}.
\]
Multiplication by the actual product
\(\eta^n(-1)^sY_J^sX_I^t\), together with the additional
cofactor factors in the ratio, proves (Cof.18) as a polynomial
identity.

Since \(H\) is odd in (Cof.7), the total power of \(\eta\) is
\(H-1\), which is even. Since \(H\) is even in (Cof.10), its
total power is \(H\), also even. Therefore the specialized
highest polynomials are exactly
\[
\boxed{
F_{n,H}=(-1)^{s+1}S^{H-n}ZR
              X_I^{t-1}Y_J^{s-1},\qquad
G_{n,H}=S^{H-2n}X_I^{2t}Y_J^{2s}.}
\tag{Cof.19}
\]
The first identity includes \(H=n+1\), using the polynomial
division already proved. These evaluations prove that both
highest vectors are nonzero whenever their displayed parameters
apply.

## 5. Proof of the canonical image assertions

Set \(n=a=r+1\), \(H=r^2+1\), \(b=H-2\), and \(W=V^*\).
The exact R-022 annihilator construction gives
\[
\delta:\mathcal K_{a,b}(W)\hookrightarrow
\ker T_{r,r,b}(W)\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^bW.
\tag{Cof.20}
\]
Indeed its only lower-map input is \(h_{b-r,r}\) surjective.
Here
\[
b-r=r^2-r-1\ge(r-1)^2
\]
for every \(r\ge2\), with equality at \(r=2\). This is Sra's
Theorem 1.3 in precisely its proved range; the freeing and
polarization maps and scalars are K.16–K.22, also P.9–P.16.

Suppose first that \(r\) is even. Use \(F_{a,H}\), choose
\[
s=(r+2)/2,\qquad t=r/2,\qquad K=\{a\}\subset I,
\]
and choose the reference slot in \(I\setminus\{a\}\).
Keep the last slot's first coordinate equal to one. Give each of
the first \(r\) slots first coordinate zero, and polarize these
slots in the common direction \(e_1\). Their resulting first
coordinates are \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\).

The required value of \((T_{r,r,b}\otimes\mathrm{id})\delta F\)
is the coefficient of \(u_1^r\cdots u_r^r\).
The first-row homogeneity \(H=r^2+1\) says that it is the
coefficient of \(x_1^r\cdots x_r^r x_a\) in (Cof.19). The factor
\(Z=x_a\) already supplies that last degree. Set \(Z=0\) in
the remaining factors. Since \(s-1=t=r/2\), this coefficient is
\[
\boxed{
(-1)^{s+1}
\binom{r^2-r}{\,r(r-1)/2\,}
\frac{\bigl((r^2/2)!\bigr)^2}{(r!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{Cof.21}
\]
The binomial splits the two group sums; their multinomial
coefficients supply the two displayed factorials. Every lower
factorial argument is nonnegative.

For odd \(r\ge3\), use \(G_{a,H}\), and let \(s=t=(r+1)/2\),
with the last slot in \(I\). The same coefficient extraction
applied to the second expression in (Cof.19) gives
\[
\boxed{
\binom{r^2-2r-1}{\,r(r-3)/2\,}
\frac{\bigl(r(r-1)/2+1\bigr)!\,
      \bigl(r(r+1)/2\bigr)!}{(r!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{Cof.22}
\]
The remaining exponent in the binomial is
\((r+1)(r-2)/2\ge0\), and its upper argument is at least two.
The group containing the last slot has total degree
\(r(r-1)/2+1\); its last coordinate has exponent one, giving the
first numerator factorial and denominator \((r!)^{s-1}\).
The other group gives the second numerator factorial and
denominator \((r!)^t\).

Equations (Cof.21) and (Cof.22) show that the unique source
highest line of the respective type in the annihilator ambient
space is not killed by the map in (Cof.20). The multiplicity-one
proof in §3 and equivariance imply that no copy of that type is
in \(\mathcal K_{a,b}\). The exact transpose pairing of (P.6)
proves (Cof.4).

## 6. Two infinite common-polarization families

The same polynomials prove additional parameter families directly
for \(T_{r,L,rL-1}\).

For every \(r\ge3\), \(L\ge1\) with \(rL\) even, set
\[
H=rL+1,\qquad
\lambda=(H,(H-1)^{r-3},H-3,H-r).
\tag{Cof.23}
\]
This source type has multiplicity one and \(T_{r,L,rL-1}\)
is injective on it. Put \(s=\lceil r/2\rceil\), \(t=\lfloor r/2\rfloor\),
choose \(K=\{1\}\subset I\), and take first-row base \(x_1=1\),
all other first-row bases zero. Formula (Cof.19) shows that
the common-polarization coefficient is
\[
\boxed{
(-1)^{s+1}(L+1)
\frac{((s-1)L)!\,(tL)!}{(L!)^{r-1}}
\binom{r(L-1)+1}{\,sL-t\,}
\binom{sL-1}{L}\ne0.}
\tag{Cof.24}
\]
To derive this exact expression, first use first-row homogeneity:
the coefficient at exponent \(L\) in every slot after translation
of the first coordinate by one is \(L+1\) times the coefficient
at exponents \((L+1,L,\ldots,L)\) before translation. Expand
\(X_I^{t-1}=(Z+R)^{t-1}\) in (Cof.19). The resulting finite
binomial sum is
\[
\sum_j\binom{t-1}{j}
\frac{1}{(L-j)!\,((s-1)L-t+j)!}
=\frac{\binom{sL-1}{L}}{(sL-t)!},
\tag{Cof.25}
\]
where terms with negative factorial arguments are zero.
This is the elementary coefficient identity for
\((1+z)^{t-1}(1+z)^{sL-t}\). The remaining group multinomials
give (Cof.24). Its arguments are all valid: at \(L=1\), parity
forces even \(r\ge4\), so \(s=t\ge2\); for odd \(r\), \(L\)
is even and at least two. In every case \(sL-t\ge0\),
\(tL-s+1\ge0\), and \(sL-1\ge L\).

For every odd \(r\ge3\) and odd \(L\ge3\), put
\[
H=rL+1,\qquad \lambda=(H^{r-1},H-2r).
\tag{Cof.26}
\]
This source type again has multiplicity one and is mapped
injectively. Use \(G_{r,H}\), \(s=(r-1)/2\), \(t=(r+1)/2\),
and put the first-row base one in a slot of \(I\). The exact value is
\[
\boxed{
\binom{rL+1-2r}{\,sL+1-2t\,}
\frac{(sL+1)!\,(tL)!}{(L!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{Cof.27}
\]
The other binomial argument is \(tL-2s\). They are nonnegative
for every displayed \(r,L\), including \(r=L=3\).
This follows directly from the second product in (Cof.19).

For these families the polynomial-generator construction uses
exactly \(r\) coordinate rows. Inclusion into larger vector
spaces commutes with coefficient extraction and the Schur
realizations. A map nonzero on a multiplicity-one irreducible
component is injective on it in every dimension where it exists.
This proves all ambient-rank statements in §§1 and 6.


# Explicit canonical image families below the square bound

Statement **R-026**. Written on 21 November 2026 UTC by GPT-6 Astra Pro,
agent /root/rectangular_cases; effort setting not exposed. The proof
uses the actual canonical map, its transpose annihilator, and explicit
highest polynomials. No historical novelty claim is made.

## 1. The two unconditional parameter families

For integers \(r\ge3\), set \(a=r+1\). The canonical map is the
normalized grid transpose followed by symmetric projection:
\[
h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b(\operatorname{Sym}^a V)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^b V).
\tag{BS.1}
\]
In every dimension at least the number of positive parts in the
displayed partition, the following assertions hold.

**Even \(r\ge4\).** For every integer \(2\le k\le r-1\), put
\[
b=r^2-k,\qquad
\lambda=((r^2)^r,\ r^2-k(r+1)).
\tag{BS.2}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{im}h_{b,a}]
=[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^b V]=1.}
\tag{BS.3}
\]

**Odd \(r\ge3\).** For every integer \(2\le k\le r-1\), put
\[
b=r^2-k,\qquad
\lambda=(r^2,(r^2-1)^{r-2},\ r^2-3,
                         \ r^2-(k-1)(r+1)).
\tag{BS.4}
\]
The same equality (BS.3) holds.

At \(k=r-1\), the last part in (BS.2) is one; at its other
parameters it is at least \(r+2\). The last part in (BS.4) is
always at least \(r+2\). These are no larger than the preceding part, so the
formulas are partitions. Their sizes are respectively
\((r+1)(r^2-k)=ab\). Their first row is exactly \(r^2\).

For example:

| \(a\) | \(b\) | \(\lambda\) |
|---:|---:|---|
| 4 | 7 | \((9,8,6,5)\) |
| 5 | 14 | \((16,16,16,16,6)\) |
| 5 | 13 | \((16,16,16,16,1)\) |
| 6 | 23 | \((25,24,24,24,22,19)\) |
| 6 | 22 | \((25,24,24,24,22,13)\) |
| 6 | 21 | \((25,24,24,24,22,7)\) |
| 7 | 34 | \((36,36,36,36,36,36,22)\) |
| 7 | 33 | \((36,36,36,36,36,36,15)\) |
| 7 | 32 | \((36,36,36,36,36,36,8)\) |
| 7 | 31 | \((36,36,36,36,36,36,1)\) |
| 8 | 43 | \((49,48,48,48,48,48,46,9)\) |

Both parity families reach every degree from \(r^2-r+1\) to
\(r^2-2\). The partitions and actual image
multiplicities at all these parameters are the formulas above.

## 2. General cofactor highest polynomials

Use an \(n\)-by-\(n\) matrix of independent variables \(X\), with
\(n\ge3\). Set
\[
D=\det X,\qquad x_j=X_{1j},\qquad
y_j=C_{nj},\qquad z_j=C_{n-1,j},
\quad
\mathcal S=\sum_j x_jz_j^2\prod_{i\ne j}y_i,
\tag{BS.5}
\]
where \(C_{ij}\) is the signed cofactor. All these are literal
polynomials with integral coefficients.

For every **even \(H\ge nk\)** and every \(k\ge1\), define
\[
G_{n,H,k}=D^{H-nk}\prod_{j=1}^n y_j^k.
\tag{BS.6}
\]
It has separate slot degree \(H-k\), row weight
\[
\lambda^G=(H^{n-1},H-nk),
\tag{BS.7}
\]
and is symmetric in the slots. Indeed a column permutation acts on
\(D\) by its sign and on the cofactor row by its sign times the
same entry permutation; the resulting character is
\(\operatorname{sgn}^{H-nk+nk}=1\).

For every **odd \(H\ge n(k-1)+1\)** and every \(k\ge2\), define
\[
F_{n,H,k}
=D^{H-n(k-1)-2}\mathcal S\prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{k-2}.
\tag{BS.8}
\]
The exponent of \(D\) is at least minus one. The quotient at that
endpoint is an actual polynomial: \(D\mid\mathcal S\), as proved
in Cof.6–Cof.9. Explicitly, on the generic rank-\((n-1)\) locus,
\(z_j=c y_j\), so \(\mathcal S=c^2\prod_i y_i\sum_jx_jy_j=0\)
by the cofactor identity. Irreducibility of the determinant then
gives divisibility in the polynomial ring.

The separate slot degree of (BS.8) is \(H-k\), and its row weight is
\[
\lambda^F=(H,(H-1)^{n-3},H-3,H-n(k-1)).
\tag{BS.9}
\]
Its slot-permutation character is
\[
\operatorname{sgn}^{H-n(k-1)-2+n+1+n(k-2)}
=\operatorname{sgn}^{H-1}=1.
\tag{BS.10}
\]
These are highest polynomials under the same actual transvections
as R-025: for \(i<j\), the substitution
\(X\mapsto(I+tE_{j,i})X\) fixes \(D\), \(x\), and \(y\).
Only \(z\mapsto z-t y\) can affect \(\mathcal S\), and its
change is
\[
-2t\Bigl(\prod y_i\Bigr)\sum_jx_jz_j
+t^2\Bigl(\prod y_i\Bigr)\sum_jx_jy_j=0.
\tag{BS.11}
\]
Thus the displayed polynomials are actual highest vectors once
their nonzero evaluations below are supplied.

## 3. The exact complement morphism and multiplicity one

For \(\lambda\) in the \(n\)-by-\(H\) rectangle, let
\(\nu=(H-\lambda_n,\ldots,H-\lambda_1)\). The exterior-column
pairing of Cof.12 is a nonzero perfect equivariant pairing
\[
S_\lambda\mathbf Q^n\otimes S_\nu\mathbf Q^n
\longrightarrow(\det\mathbf Q^n)^H.
\tag{BS.12}
\]
It pairs the content \(((H-k)^n)\) perfectly with content
\((k^n)\), because their diagonal weights add to \((H^n)\).
On the right permutation matrices act by \(\operatorname{sgn}^H\).
Taking the invariant or alternating projector on the second content
space, and applying the literal Cauchy decomposition of matrix
polynomials, gives
\[
[S_\lambda:\operatorname{Sym}^n\operatorname{Sym}^{H-k}]
=
\begin{cases}
[S_\nu:\operatorname{Sym}^n\operatorname{Sym}^{k}],&H\text{ even},\\
[S_\nu:\Lambda^n\operatorname{Sym}^{k}],&H\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\tag{BS.13}
\]
Precisely, the content-\((k^n)\) matrix-polynomial space is
\((\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathbf Q^n)^{\otimes n}\). The projectors
are \(n!^{-1}\sum_\sigma\sigma\) and
\(n!^{-1}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma\);
their normalized symmetric and alternating inclusions are the maps
used in (BS.13).

For (BS.7), the complement is the row \((nk)\). Its only weight
vector of that weight is \((e_1^k)^n\), so the required symmetric
plethysm multiplicity is one.

For (BS.9), the complement is
\[
\nu=(n(k-1),3,1^{n-3},0).
\tag{BS.14}
\]
Its entire weight space in \(\Lambda^n\operatorname{Sym}^k\)
is one-dimensional. Here is a direct count. No chosen monomial
uses the last variable. The total degree away from the first
variable is \(n\). Among distinct degree-\(k\) monomials in the
first \(n-1\) variables, there is one with that degree zero, and
there are \(n-2\) with that degree one. For \(n\) distinct
monomials, the minimum sum of those degrees is consequently
\(0+(n-2)+2=n\). Equality forces all of those first \(n-1\)
monomials and a single monomial of degree two away from the first
variable. The remaining specified weights force it to be
\(e_1^{k-2}e_2^2\). Thus the unique wedge is
\[
e_1^k\wedge e_1^{k-1}e_2\wedge\cdots\wedge
e_1^{k-1}e_{n-1}\wedge e_1^{k-2}e_2^2.
\tag{BS.15}
\]
Every raising replacement of a variable produces a repeated wedge
factor or zero, so this is a highest vector. Hence (BS.14) occurs
once and (BS.13) proves multiplicity one for (BS.9).

## 4. Exact specialization and coefficients

Use exactly the integral matrix construction in Cof.15–Cof.17.
Partition the \(n\) slots into nonempty groups \(I,J\) of sizes
\(s,t\); choose a reference \(q\in I\). Let \(A\) be the
specified unimodular matrix whose last row is the indicator of
\(J\) in the coordinates excluding \(q\). For \(F\), choose
\(p\in I\setminus\{q\}\), put \(e_p\) in the penultimate row,
and use the remaining coordinate rows before these last two rows.
With \(B=A^{-T}B_0\), where the rows of \(B_0\) are
\(e_i-e_q\), form the matrix whose first row is \(x\) and whose
lower rows are \(B\). Write
\[
X_I=\sum_{i\in I}x_i,\quad Y_J=\sum_{j\in J}x_j,\quad
S=X_I+Y_J,\quad Z=x_p,\quad R=X_I-Z.
\]
The exact cofactor identities are
\[
\begin{gathered}
D=\eta S,\quad y_i/\eta=-Y_J\ (i\in I),\quad y_j/\eta=X_I\ (j\in J),\\
\mathcal S=\eta^{n+1}(-1)^{s+1}S^2ZR X_I^{t-1}Y_J^{s-1},\quad\eta\in\{1,-1\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{BS.16}
\]
Substitution in (BS.6) and (BS.8) gives, with all signs retained,
\[
\boxed{G_{n,H,k}=(-1)^{sk}S^{H-nk}X_I^{kt}Y_J^{ks},}
\tag{BS.17}
\]
\[
\boxed{F_{n,H,k}=(-1)^{s(k-1)+1}
S^{H-n(k-1)}ZR X_I^{t(k-1)-1}Y_J^{s(k-1)-1}.}
\tag{BS.18}
\]
The powers of \(\eta\) are \(H\) and \(H-1\), respectively,
and are even in their stated ranges. These formulas are polynomial
identities, including the quotient endpoint in (BS.8).

For the canonical families, take \(n=r+1\), \(H=r^2\),
and put the last slot in \(I\). Give all slots first-row base
zero. In the first \(r\) slots, polarize in the common direction
\(e_1\); keep the last slot fixed. The required value is the
coefficient of
\[
x_1^r\cdots x_r^r x_{r+1}^{\,0}.
\tag{BS.19}
\]
Thus set \(x_{r+1}=0\) in (BS.17) or (BS.18). This base choice
is allowed: the lower rows are the explicit constant matrix \(B\),
and the polarization coefficient is a polynomial evaluation at it.

For **even \(r\ge4\)** and \(2\le k\le r-2\), use
\[
s=r/2+1,\quad t=r/2,\quad h=r^2-k(r+1),\quad
u=r(r-k)/2.
\]
There are \(r/2\) unfixed variables in each group. Formula (BS.17)
therefore gives exactly
\[
\boxed{(-1)^{sk}\binom hu
\frac{((r^2/2)!)^2}{(r!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{BS.20}
\]
Indeed the group degrees are both \(r^2/2\), so the required
power of \(X_I\) from \(S^h\) is \(u\), and the remaining
degree is \(h-u=r^2/2-k(r/2+1)\). This is at least two for all
the displayed parameters. Both multinomial coefficients are the
displayed factorial ratios. This proves the nonzero value including
the endpoint \(k=r-2\).

For **odd \(r\ge5\)** and \(2\le k\le r-1\), use
\[
s=t=(r+1)/2,\quad h=r^2-(k-1)(r+1),\quad
d_I=r(s-1),\quad d_J=rt,\quad
u=s(r-k-1).
\tag{BS.21}
\]
Choose \(p\) in the first \(r\) slots of \(I\), and take the
last slot as reference \(q\). There are \(s-1\ge2\) first
\(r\) slots in \(I\), so after setting the last coordinate zero,
\(R\) still contains at least one variable. Formula (BS.18) gives
the exact coefficient
\[
\boxed{(-1)^{s(k-1)+1}\binom hu
\binom{d_I-2}{r-1}
\frac{(d_I-r)!\,d_J!}{(r!)^{r-1}}\ne0.}
\tag{BS.22}
\]
To obtain it, the \(S^h\) split must contribute
\(X_I^uY_J^{h-u}\), since
\(u=d_I-t(k-1)-1\). The resulting first-group factor is
\(ZR(Z+R)^{d_I-2}\). Its \(Z^r\) coefficient is
\(\binom{d_I-2}{r-1}R^{d_I-r}\). The remaining first-group
variables have exponent \(r\) each, as do the \(t\) variables
of the second group, giving the two multinomial coefficients.
Every argument is valid: \(u\ge0\),
\(h-u=s(r-k+1)+1>0\), and \(d_I-r=r(s-2)\ge0\).
The binomial \(\binom{d_I-2}{r-1}\) is positive because
\(s-1\ge2\) and \(r\ge5\).

The odd endpoint \(r=3,k=2\) is also explicit. Choose
\(s=3,t=1\), put the last slot in \(I\), and choose \(p\)
among its first two slots. Then \(h=5,d_I=6,d_J=3,u=4\).
The same coefficient extraction is
\[
\binom54\binom42\frac{3!\,3!}{(3!)^2}=30\ne0.
\tag{BS.23}
\]

## 5. The even-r endpoint by an explicit apolar evaluation

Let \(r\ge4\) be even and take \(k=r-1\), \(n=r+1\),
\(H=r^2\). The polynomial (BS.6) at this endpoint is
\[
G_{n,H,r-1}=D\prod_{j=1}^{r+1}y_j^{r-1},\qquad
\lambda=((r^2)^r,1).
\tag{BS.24}
\]
We give another concrete matrix evaluation of its coefficient (BS.19).
Let \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_r\) be the distinct roots of
\(z^r+1\), put \(a_i=1+\zeta_i\), and set \(a_{r+1}=0\).
The first \(r\) values are distinct and nonzero: \(-1\) is not
a root of \(z^r+1\) for even \(r\). They therefore give the
explicit nonzero determinant matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_1^2&\cdots&a_r^2\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
a_1^r&\cdots&a_r^r\\
a_1&\cdots&a_r
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det A=(-1)^{r-1}\Bigl(\prod_i a_i\Bigr)
                       \prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)\ne0.
\tag{BS.25}
\]
Take \(B_0=(I_r\mid-\mathbf1)\), \(B=A^{-T}B_0\), and
use \(B\) for the lower rows of \(X\). This specifies the actual
matrix over the splitting field. No unimodular normalization is
made in this evaluation. Write
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^r x_i,\qquad Z=\sum_{i=1}^r a_i x_i,
\qquad \eta=(\det A)^{-1}.
\]
After setting \(x_{r+1}=0\), the determinant and cofactor identities
give exactly
\[
D=\eta S,\qquad y_i=\eta(a_iS-Z)\ (1\le i\le r),
\qquad y_{r+1}=-\eta Z.
\tag{BS.26}
\]
For the determinant, the matrix \(B_0\) gives
\((-1)^r\sum x_i\); its lower row transformation has determinant
\((\det A)^{-1}\). Since \(r\) is even, this is the stated
\(\eta\). The cofactor formulas follow from \(C=DX^{-T}\),
exactly as in Cof.16, with the last row of \(A\) equal to \(a\).

Let
\[
Q(s,z)=\prod_{i=1}^r(z-a_i s)=(z-s)^r+s^r,
\qquad Q_0(s,z)=z^r+s^r.
\]
Substituting (BS.26) into (BS.24) gives the exact binary expression
\[
G_{n,H,r-1}=-\eta^{r^2}S Z^{r-1}Q(S,Z)^{r-1}.
\tag{BS.27}
\]
For degree-\(N\) binary forms define the bilinear pairing
\[
\langle P,R\rangle_N
=\left.P(-\partial_z,\partial_s)R(s,z)\right|_{s=z=0}.
\tag{BS.28}
\]
The chain rule for the two displayed linear forms \(S,Z\) identifies
the required coefficient, with its full normalization, as
\[
[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r]G_{n,H,r-1}
=-\frac{\eta^{r^2}}{(r!)^r}
\left\langle Q^r,\ s z^{r-1}Q^{r-1}\right\rangle_{r^2}.
\tag{BS.29}
\]
Indeed differentiation in \(x_i\) acts as
\(\partial_s+a_i\partial_z\); the product of its \(r\)-th
powers is exactly \(Q(-\partial_z,\partial_s)^r\).
The factor \((r!)^{-r}\) is the ordinary monomial coefficient
normalization.

The substitution \(\tau R(s,z)=R(s,z-s)\) preserves the pairing
(BS.28). This follows directly from the chain rule:
\((\partial_s+\partial_z)\tau R=\tau(\partial_sR)\) and
\(\partial_z\tau R=\tau(\partial_zR)\). Substitution in
\((\tau P)(-\partial_z,\partial_s)
=P(-\partial_z,\partial_s+\partial_z)\), followed by evaluation
at zero, proves \(\langle\tau P,\tau R\rangle=\langle P,R\rangle\).
Applying this actual change of variables to (BS.29) gives
\[
\left\langle Q^r,s z^{r-1}Q^{r-1}\right\rangle_{r^2}
=\left\langle Q_0^r,s(z+s)^{r-1}Q_0^{r-1}\right\rangle_{r^2}.
\tag{BS.30}
\]
Every exponent of \(s\) or \(z\) in a monomial of \(Q_0^r\)
is a multiple of \(r\). In the extra factor
\(s(z+s)^{r-1}\), the \(z\)-exponent lies between zero and
\(r-1\). Consequently only its term \(s^r\) can pair
nontrivially with \(Q_0^r\) after multiplication by \(Q_0^{r-1}\).
Expanding these two binomial powers now gives
\[
\boxed{[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r]G_{n,H,r-1}
=-\frac{\eta^{r^2}}{(r!)^r}
\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\binom ri\binom{r-1}{i}
(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!\ne0.}
\tag{BS.31}
\]
The differential sign in each term is \((-1)^{ri}=1\), since
\(r\) is even. Every integer summand is positive and
\(\eta\ne0\). This proves the endpoint for every even \(r\)
in the statement, by a fully specified algebraic evaluation of the
same integral highest polynomial. The field inclusion from \(\mathbf Q\)
into this splitting field is injective. A zero polynomial image over
\(\mathbf Q\) remains zero after that scalar extension, so the
nonzero value detects the original map as well.

## 6. Transfer to the actual canonical image

Let \(W=V^*\), and let \(\mathcal K_{a,b}(W)\) be the
annihilator of the image of (BS.1) under the normalized symmetric
tensor pairing. The actual last-slot inclusion and coefficient
polarization from K.16–K.22 give
\[
\delta\mathcal K_{a,b}(W)
\subset\ker T_{r,r,b}(W)\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^bW
\tag{BS.32}
\]
throughout both displayed families. To verify its lower-map input,
\[
b-r-(r-1)^2=r-k-1\ge0.
\tag{BS.33}
\]
Thus Sra's Theorem 1.3 proves that the actual lower canonical map
\(h_{b-r,r}\) is surjective at every parameter used here.

The inclusion \(\delta\) is the normalized last-slot splitting
of a symmetric \((r+1)\)-tensor; polynomial evaluation on symmetric
slot functions identifies it with retaining the same polynomial
and distinguishing the last variable. The map \(T_{r,r,b}\)
extracts the coefficient of \(u_1^r\cdots u_r^r\) after the
substitution \(v_i\mapsto v_i+u_i x\) in its first \(r\) slots.
These are the literal maps of (BS.32). The derivation, including
the nonzero factorial and binomial scalars in the annihilator
inclusion, is K.16–K.22 and P.9–P.16; (BS.33) checks precisely
its application range here.

Equations (BS.20), (BS.22), (BS.23), and (BS.31) are nonzero values of
\((T_{r,r,b}\otimes\mathrm{id})\delta\) on the respective
highest polynomials. By (BS.13)–(BS.15), each corresponding
type occurs exactly once in the entire annihilator ambient
module \(\operatorname{Sym}^{r+1}\operatorname{Sym}^bW\).
Equivariance and (BS.32) exclude that single copy from
\(\mathcal K_{a,b}\). The perfect transpose pairing therefore
proves exactly (BS.3).

All constructions use \(a\) coordinate rows. Inclusion into any
larger vector space commutes with symmetric projection, grid
transpose, column alternation, and the displayed coefficient maps.
The polynomial-functor multiplicity of each label with at most
\(a\) rows is unchanged: the highest vectors involving those
coordinate rows and their raising equations give the same Schur
multiplicity space. Hence the same nonzero canonical component
persists in every stated ambient dimension.

The lower-map source is Suvrit Sra, *The q-Foulkes problem III: On
Foulkes' conjecture with a graded inner factor*, Theorem 1.3,
[primary PDF](https://suvrit.github.io/papers/qfoulkes3/qfoulkes3-v1.pdf).
The exact range used is \(h_{B,r}\) surjective for
\(B\ge(r-1)^2\). The remaining maps, polynomial identities,
parameter arithmetic, and nonzero coefficients have been proved
explicitly above.


# Canonical image families with first row one above the polarization degree

Statement **R-027**, 21 November 2026 UTC. GPT-6 Astra Pro,
/root/rectangular_cases; effort setting not exposed.

## 1. The unconditional families

Let \(r\ge2\), \(a=r+1\), and \(H=r^2+1\). Use the actual
normalized canonical grid map
\[
h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b\operatorname{Sym}^a V
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^b V.
\tag{NR.1}
\]
For **even \(r\ge2\)** and every integer \(2\le k\le r\), put
\[
b=H-k,\qquad
\lambda=(H,(H-1)^{r-2},H-3,H-(k-1)(r+1)).
\tag{NR.2}
\]
For **odd \(r\ge3\)** and every integer \(2\le k\le r-1\), put
\[
b=H-k,\qquad
\lambda=(H^r,H-k(r+1)).
\tag{NR.3}
\]
For both families, in every dimension at least the number of positive
parts of \(\lambda\),
\[
\boxed{[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{im}h_{b,a}]
=[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^b V]=1.}
\tag{NR.4}
\]
All displayed labels are partitions of \(ab\). Their last part is
at least two; their first row is exactly \(r^2+1\). Family (NR.2)
covers every \(b\) from \(r^2-r+1\) through \(r^2-1\), and
(NR.3) covers every \(b\) from \(r^2-r+2\) through \(r^2-1\).
At \(k=2\) these are exactly R-025's two canonical families.
No historical novelty claim is made.

## 2. The highest vectors and the canonical transfer

Retain the literal determinant, cofactor rows, and polynomial
\(\mathcal S\) of BS.5:
\[
D=\det X,\qquad y_j=C_{a,j},\qquad z_j=C_{a-1,j},\qquad
\mathcal S=\sum_jX_{1j}z_j^2\prod_{i\ne j}y_i.
\]
Use the integral highest polynomials
\[
F_{a,H,k}=D^{H-a(k-1)-2}\mathcal S\prod_jy_j^{k-2}
\quad\text{for (NR.2)},
\tag{NR.5}
\]
\[
G_{a,H,k}=D^{H-ak}\prod_jy_j^k
\quad\text{for (NR.3)}.
\tag{NR.6}
\]
The determinant exponents in this report are nonnegative. Their slot
degrees, row weights, highest transvections, and symmetric slot actions
are proved by the explicit maps BS.5–BS.11. Their multiplicity is
exactly one by the perfect exterior-column pairing BS.12 and the literal
symmetric or alternating projectors BS.13. For \(F\), its complementary
highest weight is \((a(k-1),3,1^{a-3},0)\), and the unique wedge is
BS.15. For \(G\), the complement is the single row \((ak)\).
These are precise applications of those already proved maps, with
\(a=r+1\), \(H=r^2+1\), and separate slot degree \(H-k=b\).

Let \(\delta\) distinguish the last slot of the dual target, and
let \(T_{r,r,b}\) extract the common-polarization coefficient
\([u_1^r\cdots u_r^r]\) in the first \(r\) slots. The actual
annihilator inclusion of BS.32 applies throughout (NR.2)–(NR.3), since
\[
b-r-(r-1)^2=r-k\ge0.
\tag{NR.7}
\]
Its lower canonical map \(h_{b-r,r}\) is therefore surjective by
Sra's Theorem 1.3 in its stated range. To exclude the multiplicity-one
highest line from that annihilator, it suffices to give a nonzero
value of \((T_{r,r,b}\otimes\mathrm{id})\delta\) on the actual
polynomial (NR.5) or (NR.6).

Give the first \(r\) slots first-row base zero and the last slot
first-row base one, and use common direction \(e_1\). Since the
first-row degree is \(H=r^2+1\), the resulting value is exactly
\[
[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r x_{r+1}]F_{a,H,k}
\quad\text{or}\quad
[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r x_{r+1}]G_{a,H,k}.
\tag{NR.8}
\]
The last-slot inclusion is normalized so that its evaluation on a
symmetric slot polynomial retains the same polynomial. Thus no extra
slot factorial occurs in (NR.8).

## 3. The interior parameters by exact group-sum coefficients

Use the same explicit unimodular matrices BS.16–BS.18; let the last
slot belong to \(I\), with group sizes \(s,t\).

For even \(r\ge4\) and \(2\le k\le r-1\), take
\[
s=r/2+1,\quad t=r/2,\quad
h=H-(r+1)(k-1),\quad u=r(r-k+1)/2,
\]
and choose the distinguished slot \(p=r+1\). Its coordinate \(Z\)
already supplies the power one of the last variable in BS.18, so set
that variable zero in every other factor. The exact coefficient is
\[
\boxed{(-1)^{s(k-1)+1}\binom hu
\frac{((r^2/2)!)^2}{(r!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{NR.9}
\]
Both groups then have \(r/2\) first slots, each with required degree
\(r\). The fixed powers of their sums are \(t(k-1)\) and
\(s(k-1)-1\); the remaining split of \(S^h\) is \((u,h-u)\).
The second quantity is
\(r^2/2-s(k-1)+1\ge3\), so every factorial and binomial argument
in (NR.9) is valid and its magnitude is positive.

For odd \(r\ge5\) and \(2\le k\le r-2\), take
\[
s=t=(r+1)/2,\quad h=H-(r+1)k,\quad
d_I=r(s-1)+1,\quad d_J=rt,\quad u=d_I-kt.
\]
The last coordinate has exponent one inside the first group, while its
other \(s-1\) variables and all \(t\) second-group variables have
exponent \(r\). Formula BS.17 gives exactly
\[
\boxed{(-1)^{sk}\binom hu
\frac{d_I!\,d_J!}{(r!)^r}\ne0.}
\tag{NR.10}
\]
Here \(u\ge2\), with equality at \(k=r-2\), and
\(h-u=s(r-k)>0\). These inequalities verify every endpoint of this
interior range. The two remaining endpoint constructions follow.

## 4. The even-r endpoint: a positive apolar sum

Let \(r\ge2\) be even and take \(k=r\). Then the highest
polynomial and label are
\[
F_{r+1,H,r}=\mathcal S\prod_jy_j^{r-2},\qquad
\lambda=(r^2+1,(r^2)^{r-2},r^2-2,2).
\tag{NR.11}
\]
Choose the distinct roots \(\zeta_i\) of \(z^r+1\) and put
\(a_i=1+\zeta_i\) for \(1\le i\le r\), \(a_{r+1}=0\).
Also put \(b_i=0\) for \(i\le r\), and \(b_{r+1}=1\).
Take reference slot \(q=1\). In the coordinates excluding slot one,
define the \(r\)-by-\(r\) matrix \(A\) by these rows in order:
\[
(a_i^2-a_1^2)_i,\ldots,(a_i^{r-1}-a_1^{r-1})_i,
\qquad (b_i)_i,\qquad(a_i-a_1)_i.
\tag{NR.12}
\]
The first list is empty at \(r=2\). Expanding along the \(b\)-row
leaves a nonzero Vandermonde determinant on \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\):
divide each remaining column by \(a_i-a_1\), and use the monic
polynomials \((T^j-a_1^j)/(T-a_1)\), of distinct degrees
\(0,\ldots,r-2\). This proves \(\det A\ne0\) with the actual
matrix (NR.12).

Let \(B_0\) have rows \(e_i-e_1\), \(i\ne1\), in increasing
order, and put \(B=A^{-T}B_0\) in the lower rows of \(X\).
Write \(\eta=(\det A)^{-1}\),
\(S=\sum_{i\le r}x_i\), \(Z=\sum_{i\le r}a_i x_i\),
and \(w=x_{r+1}\). Direct cofactor evaluation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D&=\eta(S+w),& y_i&=\eta((S+w)a_i-Z)\quad(i\le r),\\
y_{r+1}&=-\eta Z,&z_i&=-\eta w\quad(i\le r),&
z_{r+1}&=\eta S.
\end{aligned}
\tag{NR.13}
\]
For this reference slot, \(\det(x;B_0)=\sum x_i\), fixing the
displayed scalar. Shifting all entries of \(a\) by \(-a_1\)
does not change \((\sum x_i)a_j-\sum_i a_i x_i\); this proves
the last-row formula from the row in (NR.12), including the omitted
reference coordinate. The same calculation applies to \(b\).

In the numerator \(\mathcal S\), each summand indexed by a first
slot has the factor \(z_i^2=\eta^2w^2\). Therefore only the
last summand contributes to \([w]\) of (NR.11). With
\(Q(s,z)=(z-s)^r+s^r\), it gives exactly
\[
[w]F_{r+1,H,r}=\eta^{r^2} S^2 Z^{r-2}Q(S,Z)^{r-1}.
\tag{NR.14}
\]
All cofactor signs cancel here: their total exponent of minus one is
\(r(r-1)+r-2=r^2-2\), even for this range of \(r\).

Use the exact pairing
\(\langle P,R\rangle_N=P(-\partial_z,\partial_s)R|_0\)
of BS.28. The chain rule and normalized coefficient extraction give
\[
[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r w]F_{r+1,H,r}
=\frac{\eta^{r^2}}{(r!)^r}
\left\langle Q^r,s^2z^{r-2}Q^{r-1}\right\rangle_{r^2}.
\tag{NR.15}
\]
Under the actual substitution \(z\mapsto z-s\), the chain-rule
invariance proved in BS.28–BS.30 transforms this pairing into
\[
\left\langle Q_0^r,s^2(z+s)^{r-2}Q_0^{r-1}\right\rangle_{r^2},
\qquad Q_0=z^r+s^r.
\]
Only the term with \(z\)-exponent zero in the extra factor can
pair with a monomial of \(Q_0^r\): all its exponents are divisible
by \(r\), whereas that extra exponent is between zero and \(r-2\).
The surviving factor is \(s^r\). Hence the exact value is
\[
\boxed{\frac{\eta^{r^2}}{(r!)^r}
\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\binom ri\binom{r-1}{i}
(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!\ne0.}
\tag{NR.16}
\]
Every summand is a positive integer, and \(\eta\ne0\). This
also proves the \(r=2\) case of the statement.

## 5. The odd-r endpoint: an exact factorial inequality

Let \(r\ge3\) be odd and take \(k=r-1\). Now
\[
G_{r+1,H,r-1}=D^2\prod_jy_j^{r-1},\qquad
\lambda=((r^2+1)^r,2).
\tag{NR.17}
\]
Choose \(a_i=2+\zeta_i\), where the \(\zeta_i\) are the
distinct roots of \(z^r+1\), and put \(a_{r+1}=0\).
The \(a_i\) are distinct and nonzero. With reference slot \(r+1\),
take the matrix whose rows are \((a_i^2)_i,\ldots,(a_i^r)_i,(a_i)_i\),
and again use \(B=A^{-T}(I_r\mid-\mathbf1)\). This is the
explicit nonzero Vandermonde matrix of BS.25. Since \(r\) is odd,
the exact determinant scalar is
\(\eta=-(\det A)^{-1}\).

Set \(S=\sum_{i\le r}x_i\), \(Z=\sum_{i\le r}a_i x_i\),
and \(w=x_{r+1}\). The same literal cofactors now give
\[
G_{r+1,H,r-1}=\eta^H(S+w)^2 Z^{r-1}Q(S+w,Z)^{r-1},
\qquad Q(s,z)=(z-2s)^r+s^r.
\tag{NR.18}
\]
The sign from the product of the \(r+1\) cofactor factors is one,
because \((r+1)(r-1)\) is even. Differentiation in \(w\)
acts as \(\partial_s\). Consequently the exact coefficient is
\[
\frac{\eta^H}{(r!)^r}
\left\langle zQ^r,s^2z^{r-1}Q^{r-1}\right\rangle_H.
\tag{NR.19}
\]
The extra factor \(z\) in the first argument gives precisely this
\(\partial_s\) in the apolar differential operator.

Translate by \(z\mapsto z-2s\). The pairing in (NR.19) becomes
\[
\left\langle (z+2s)Q_0^r,
s^2(z+2s)^{r-1}Q_0^{r-1}\right\rangle_H,
\qquad Q_0=z^r+s^r.
\tag{NR.20}
\]
There are only two possible exponent matches modulo \(r\).
Write the extra \(s\)-exponent in the first argument as
\(\ell\in\{0,1\}\). In the second argument, the extra
\(z\)-exponent must equal \(\ell\), since it lies between
zero and \(r-1\). Expanding these two contributions gives
\[
2^{r-1}\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}(-1)^i\binom ri\binom{r-1}{i}
(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!\,(r^2-r+2-r^2 i).
\tag{NR.21}
\]
This is an exact signed intermediate expression, whose positivity
is proved next.

Define
\[
D_i=\binom ri^2(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!,\qquad
U_r=\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i(r-2i)D_i.
\tag{NR.22}
\]
The identity \(\binom{r-1}{i}=(r-i)\binom ri/r\), followed by
pairing the terms indexed by \(i\) and \(r-i\), transforms
(NR.21) exactly into
\[
2^{r-1}\frac{r^2-r+2}{2r}\,U_r.
\tag{NR.23}
\]
In this calculation \(D_{r-i}=D_i\) and
\((-1)^{r-i}=-(-1)^i\); the terms involving \(r^2i(r-i)\)
cancel. These identities prove (NR.23), including its scalar.

Here is a uniform strict lower bound. The terms \(i=0,r\) in
\(U_r\) sum to \(2r(r^2)!\). For every \(1\le i\le r-1\),
\[
\frac{D_i}{(r^2)!}
=\frac{\binom ri^2}{\binom{r^2}{ri}}
\le{\binom ri}^{2-r}\le r^{2-r}.
\tag{NR.24}
\]
The first inequality follows by selecting the term of degree \(i\)
in each of the \(r\) factors in
\((1+z)^{r^2}=((1+z)^r)^r\):
\(\binom{r^2}{ri}\ge\binom ri^r\).
The second follows from \(\binom ri\ge r\), verified by the
successive binomial ratio up to the middle and then symmetry.
Therefore the total absolute contribution of the interior terms is at
most
\[
(r-1)(r-2)r^{2-r}(r^2)!<r(r^2)!<2r(r^2)!.
\tag{NR.25}
\]
For the strict inequality, \(r\ge3\) gives
\(r^{2-r}\le1/r\) and \((r-1)(r-2)<r^2\).
It follows that \(U_r>0\). The exact endpoint coefficient is thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{\eta^H}{(r!)^r}
2^{r-1}\frac{r^2-r+2}{2r}\,U_r\ne0.}
\tag{NR.26}
\]
This establishes every odd endpoint, including \(r=3\).

## 6. Completion and scope

The nonzero values (NR.9), (NR.10), (NR.16), and (NR.26), the
multiplicity-one morphisms in §2, and the actual annihilator inclusion
with parameter check (NR.7) prove (NR.4). The explicit evaluations in
the splitting fields detect the original rational polynomial maps:
scalar extension of a zero rational vector remains zero under the
injective field map. Inclusion of coordinate rows into larger ambient
spaces commutes with every tensor projector and coefficient map, so
the same conclusions hold in every stated dimension.

The source range used in (NR.7) is Sra, *The q-Foulkes problem III:
On Foulkes' conjecture with a graded inner factor*, Theorem 1.3,
[primary PDF](https://suvrit.github.io/papers/qfoulkes3/qfoulkes3-v1.pdf).
The normalized annihilator morphism is proved in K.16–K.22 and
P.9–P.16. All polynomial and apolar comparisons used here are the
actual maps displayed above and in BS.5–BS.18, BS.28–BS.30.


# A complete strip of canonical cofactor components

## R-028. Statement

For every integer \(r\ge2\), and every integer \(j\) satisfying
\[
0\le j\le r-2,\qquad j\equiv r\pmod2,
\tag{ES.1}
\]
put
\[
a=r+1,\quad H=r^2+j,\quad b=r^2-r+1+j,
\qquad \lambda=(H^r,j+1).
\tag{ES.2}
\]
For the normalized canonical map
\[
h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b\operatorname{Sym}^a V
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^b V,
\]
the target multiplicity and image multiplicity of \(S_\lambda V\)
are both exactly one. This statement holds for every ambient vector
space in which the label exists; for smaller dimensions the Schur
functor is zero.

The even \(r\), \(j=0\) endpoint is already included in R-026,
and the odd \(r\), \(j=1\) endpoint in R-027. The proof below
establishes every parameter in (ES.1). It makes no historical
novelty claim.

## 1. Highest polynomial and the actual complement pairing

Use an \(a\times a\) matrix whose columns are the \(a\) slot
vectors. Let \(D\) be its determinant and let \(y_i=C_{a,i}\)
be its last-row cofactors. The polynomial is
\[
G=D^{j+1}\prod_{i=1}^a y_i^{r-1}.
\tag{ES.3}
\]
It is separately of degree
\((j+1)+(a-1)(r-1)=b\) in every column. Its first \(a-1=r\)
row weights are \((j+1)+a(r-1)=H\), and its last row weight
is \(j+1\). A raising substitution from an earlier row into a
later row leaves each relevant determinant or cofactor unchanged,
or produces a repeated row. Hence (ES.3) is highest of weight
\(\lambda\). A column permutation multiplies it by
\(\operatorname{sgn}^{j+1+a(r-1)}=\operatorname{sgn}^{H}=1\).
It is a nonzero symmetric slot polynomial in the indicated target.

For completeness, the multiplicity assertion uses the actual perfect
complement pairing of BS.10–BS.13. Wedge complementary column
vectors into the fixed volume tensor, then apply the primitive
Young projectors on the two tensor powers. Its perfectness identifies
\(S_\lambda\) with
\(\det^H\otimes S_{(a(r-1))}^*\). On the balanced weight
spaces it pairs content \((b^a)\) with \(((r-1)^a)\), and a
slot permutation changes the pairing by \(\operatorname{sgn}^H\).
Since \(H\) is even, the literal symmetric projectors
\(a!^{-1}\sum_\sigma\sigma\) on the two sides correspond.
Thus the target multiplicity is the multiplicity of the row
\((a(r-1))\) in
\(\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^{r-1}\).
Its highest weight space is spanned by \((e_1^{r-1})^a\), so it
has dimension one. This is the same explicit pairing and projector
construction proved in BS.10–BS.13, applied with \(k=r-1\).

## 2. The canonical annihilator map to be detected

Write \(K_{a,b}\) for the kernel of the transpose canonical map
\(h_{a,b}\); polynomial duality uses the normalized tensor
pairing of K.16–K.22. Retaining one of the \(a\) symmetric slots
defines the injective normalized map \(\delta\). The literal
coefficient-extraction map \(T_{r,r,b}\) polarizes the other
\(r\) slots by \(r\) copies of their common vector.

The exact annihilator inclusion proved in K.16–K.22 and P.9–P.16
applies here because
\[
b-r=(r-1)^2+j\ge(r-1)^2.
\tag{ES.4}
\]
Sra's Theorem 1.3 supplies surjectivity of the lower canonical map
\(h_{b-r,r}\). The specified morphisms therefore give
\[
\delta K_{a,b}\subset
\ker T_{r,r,b}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^b V^*.
\tag{ES.5}
\]
All normalized scalar factors in this inclusion are those already
computed in the cited equations. In particular none is zero.

Since the relevant target multiplicity is one, a nonzero value of
\((T_{r,r,b}\otimes1)\delta G\) proves that its entire copy lies
in the image of \(h_{b,a}\). We now compute that value. Set the
first-row bases of the first \(r\) columns to zero, polarize in
direction \(e_1\), and retain the first-row coordinate \(w\) in
the last column. The coefficient to be detected is
\[
[x_1^r\cdots x_r^r w^j]G.
\tag{ES.6}
\]
Its first-row total degree is exactly \(r^2+j=H\).

## 3. Literal cofactor specialization

Let \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_r\) be the distinct roots of
\(z^r+1\), put \(a_i=2+\zeta_i\) for \(i\le r\), and put
\(a_{r+1}=0\). All \(a_i\), \(i\le r\), are nonzero.
Form the invertible matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_1^2&\cdots&a_r^2\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
a_1^r&\cdots&a_r^r\\
a_1&\cdots&a_r
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=A^{-T}(I_r\mid-\mathbf1).
\tag{ES.7}
\]
Factoring \(a_i\) from column \(i\) leaves a permutation of the
Vandermonde exponents \(0,1,\ldots,r-1\), proving invertibility.
Use \(B\) as the lower \(r\) rows of the slot matrix. Put
\[
\eta=(-1)^r(\det A)^{-1},\quad
S=\sum_{i=1}^r x_i,\quad Z=\sum_{i=1}^r a_i x_i,
\quad Q(s,z)=(z-2s)^r+s^r.
\]
The cofactors, computed by their defining minors, are exactly
\[
D=\eta(S+w),\qquad y_i=\eta((S+w)a_i-Z).
\tag{ES.8}
\]
One direct verification is that \(B\mathbf1=0\) and
\(B(a_1,\ldots,a_r,0)^T=e_r\). The displayed cofactor row
has zero pairing with the first row and pairs with each lower row
as the determinant times the appropriate Kronecker delta; the last
first-row cofactor is \((-1)^r(\det A)^{-1}\), fixing the scalar.

Multiplying (ES.8), with every sign retained, gives
\[
G=(-1)^{r-1}\eta^H(S+w)^{j+1}Z^{r-1}
Q(S+w,Z)^{r-1}.
\tag{ES.9}
\]
Indeed \(\prod_{i\le r}(s a_i-z)=(-1)^rQ(s,z)\), while the
last cofactor contributes \((-z)^{r-1}\).

## 4. Exact binary contraction

For two binary forms of degree \(N\), use the unnormalized apolar
pairing
\[
\langle P,R\rangle_N=P(-\partial_z,\partial_s)R\big|_{s=z=0}.
\tag{ES.10}
\]
Extraction of the \(w^j\) coefficient in (ES.9) is
\(j!^{-1}\partial_s^j\). Extraction of \(x_1^r\cdots x_r^r\)
then applies
\((r!)^{-r}\prod_i(\partial_s+a_i\partial_z)^r\).
Since \(Q(-\partial_z,\partial_s)=
\prod_i(\partial_s+a_i\partial_z)\), the result is exactly
\[
\frac{(-1)^{r-1}\eta^H}{j!(r!)^r}
\left\langle z^jQ^r,
s^{j+1}z^{r-1}Q^{r-1}\right\rangle_H.
\tag{ES.11}
\]
The extra factor \(z^j\) supplies precisely \(\partial_s^j\).
The chain rule for the determinant-one substitution \(z\mapsto
z-2s\), already explicitly checked in BS.28–BS.30, changes the
pairing to
\[
\left\langle (z+2s)^jQ_0^r,
s^{j+1}(z+2s)^{r-1}Q_0^{r-1}\right\rangle_H,
\qquad Q_0=z^r+s^r.
\tag{ES.12}
\]

Choose the \(z^{ri}\) term of the first power of \(Q_0\), and
the \(z^\ell\) term of its extra factor. The other argument
must use the \(z^{r(r-i)}\) term and extra \(z^{j-\ell}\).
These are the only matches: the sum of the two extra exponents is
congruent to \(j\) modulo \(r\), lies between zero and
\(j+r-1\), and \(j<r\). Thus it equals \(j\).
In particular \(1\le i\le r\) and \(0\le\ell\le j\).
All powers of 2 multiply to \(2^{r-1}\). As \(H\) is even,
the apolar sign can be written as \((-1)^{ri+\ell}\). Therefore
(ES.12) is exactly \(2^{r-1}F_{r,j}\), where
\[
\boxed{F_{r,j}=
\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{\ell=0}^j
(-1)^{ri+\ell}
\binom ri\binom{r-1}{r-i}
\binom j\ell\binom{r-1}{j-\ell}
(ri+\ell)!\,(H-ri-\ell)!.}
\tag{ES.13}
\]
We next prove that this actual integer is strictly positive.

## 5. A uniform strict factorial bound

First take \(r\ge5\). In the endpoint \(i=r\), let
\(t_\ell\) denote the absolute value of its \(\ell\)-th term.
For \(\ell<j\),
\[
\frac{t_{\ell+1}}{t_\ell}
=\frac{(j-\ell)(r^2+\ell+1)}
       {(\ell+1)(r-j+\ell)}
\ge\frac{r^2+j}{j(r-1)}>1.
\tag{ES.14}
\]
The first factor is minimized at \(\ell=j-1\); so is the
second ratio, since its numerator minus denominator is positive
and constant. The last term has sign
\((-1)^{r^2+j}=1\). Pairing consecutive terms backwards gives
the endpoint contribution at least \(t_j-t_{j-1}\). For \(j=0\)
the same bound holds with \(t_{-1}=0\). Consequently it is at least
\[
H!\left(1-\frac{j(r-1)}{r^2+j}\right)
\ge H!\frac{4(r-1)}{r^2+r-2}.
\tag{ES.15}
\]
The last rational function decreases in \(j\), and its value at
\(j=r-2\) is the displayed lower bound.

For \(1\le i\le r-1\), selecting a term in the binomial
convolution proves
\[
\binom H{ri+\ell}
\ge\binom{r^2}{ri}\binom j\ell,
\qquad
\binom{r^2}{ri}\ge{\binom ri}^{r}.
\tag{ES.16}
\]
The second inequality selects degree \(i\) in each of the \(r\)
factors \(((1+z)^r)^r\). Also
\(\binom{r-1}{r-i}=(i/r)\binom ri\) and
\(\binom ri\ge r\). Divide the absolute terms of (ES.13) by
\(H!\), apply (ES.16), cancel \(\binom j\ell\), and sum
\(\binom{r-1}{j-\ell}\) over \(\ell\). The total absolute
interior contribution is at most
\[
H!\,(r-1)2^{r-1}r^{2-r}
<H!\frac{4(r-1)}{r^2+r-2}.
\tag{ES.17}
\]
For the strict inequality, \(r\ge5\) gives
\((2/r)^{r-2}\le(2/r)^3=8/r^3<2/(r^2+r-2)\).
The final inequality is equivalent to
\(4(r^2+r-2)<r^3\); subtracting its left side gives at least
\(r^2-4r+8=(r-2)^2+4>0\), since \(r-4\ge1\).
Equations (ES.15)–(ES.17) prove \(F_{r,j}>0\).

The remaining four pairs \((r,j)\) have the following exact
values, obtained by the finite factorial sum (ES.13):

| \((r,j)\) | \(F_{r,j}/(r!)^r\) |
|---|---:|
| \((2,0)\) | 8 |
| \((3,1)\) | 12,960 |
| \((4,0)\) | 63,705,600 |
| \((4,2)\) | 13,208,832,000 |

Each is positive. These exhaust all the parameters of (ES.1) with
\(r<5\).

## 6. Exact conclusion and verification scope

Combining (ES.11)–(ES.17), the literal coefficient (ES.6) is
\[
\boxed{\frac{(-1)^{r-1}\eta^H2^{r-1}}{j!(r!)^r}
F_{r,j}\ne0.}
\tag{ES.18}
\]
This detects the actual polarization in (ES.5). Its nonvanishing,
the one-dimensional target multiplicity, and the perfect transpose
pairing prove the claimed image multiplicity one. Extending the
coefficient field to the splitting field used in (ES.7) detects a
nonzero rational polynomial map, because field extension is
injective. Inclusion into a larger ambient vector space commutes
with the tensor projectors, retained-slot map and polarization,
giving the stated ambient-dimension transfer.

The lower-map primary source is Sra, *The q-Foulkes problem III:
On Foulkes' conjecture with a graded inner factor*, Theorem 1.3,
[primary PDF](https://suvrit.github.io/papers/qfoulkes3/qfoulkes3-v1.pdf).
The full morphism normalization is K.16–K.22 and P.9–P.16; the
complement pairing is BS.10–BS.13. These are the actual inputs,
with the new parameter verification (ES.4).

The companion audit `verify_cofactor_endpoint_strip.py` compares
fully expanded rational binary forms to (ES.13), checks literal
matrix minors and coefficient extraction over finite fields, and
records its exact receipts separately. Those calculations support
the explicit identities; the uniform nonvanishing proof is
(ES.14)–(ES.17).


# A second canonical cofactor endpoint in every even outer rank

## R-029. Statement and actual highest polynomial

For every odd integer \(r\ge3\), put
\[
a=r+1,\quad b=r^2-r+2,\quad H=r^2+2,
\qquad
\lambda=(H,(H-1)^{r-2},H-3,3).
\tag{SE.1}
\]
The normalized canonical map
\(h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b\operatorname{Sym}^aV
\to\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^bV\)
has target and image multiplicity exactly one at \(\lambda\),
in every ambient dimension where this label exists.

Use the \(a\times a\) matrix of slot vectors, its determinant
\(D\), first-row entries \(x_i\), and cofactors
\(y_i=C_{a,i}\), \(z_i=C_{a-1,i}\). Define
\[
\mathcal S=\sum_i x_i z_i^2\prod_{h\ne i}y_h,
\qquad F=D\mathcal S\prod_i y_i^{r-2}.
\tag{SE.2}
\]
This is exactly the polynomial \(F_{a,H,r}\) of BS.8. Its slot
degree is \(H-r=b\), and its row weights are those in (SE.1).
The raising substitutions and literal cofactor identities in
BS.8–BS.9 prove that it is a symmetric highest polynomial.
Here the determinant exponent is one, so no division is involved.

The perfect complementary-column pairing and primitive Young
projectors BS.10–BS.15 identify its target multiplicity with that of
\[
\nu=(a(r-1),3,1^{a-3},0)
\quad\hbox{in}\quad\Lambda^a\operatorname{Sym}^r.
\tag{SE.3}
\]
The alternation is fixed by the odd value of \(H\). The entire
weight space at (SE.3) is the single wedge of
\(e_1^r\), the \(a-2\) monomials \(e_1^{r-1}e_i\)
for \(2\le i\le a-1\), and \(e_1^{r-2}e_2^2\).
Indeed these are precisely the \(a\) distinct monomials with the
smallest possible total degree \(a\) away from the first variable;
the displayed remaining weights force the final choice. Every
raising operator produces a repeated factor or zero. Thus it is
highest and the target multiplicity is one, with the actual pairing
and alternating projector specified above.

The exact retained-slot annihilator inclusion K.16–K.22 applies,
since the lower canonical inner degree is
\[
b-r=(r-1)^2+1\ge(r-1)^2.
\tag{SE.4}
\]
Sra's Theorem 1.3 supplies that lower-map surjectivity. Consequently
the nonzero common-polarization value computed below excludes this
unique highest line from the transpose kernel and proves the
stated actual image multiplicity.

## 1. Cofactor matrix with two distinguished rows

Let \(\zeta_i\) be the distinct roots of \(z^r+1\), and set
\(a_i=2+\zeta_i\) for \(i\le r\), \(a_{r+1}=0\).
Set \(b_i=0\) for \(i\le r\), and \(b_{r+1}=1\).
Take reference column 1. With columns indexed by \(2,\ldots,r+1\),
let \(A\) have rows
\[
(a_i^2-a_1^2)_i,\ldots,(a_i^{r-1}-a_1^{r-1})_i,
\quad(b_i)_i,\quad(a_i-a_1)_i.
\tag{SE.5}
\]
This is invertible: a linear relation among its rows gives a
polynomial of degree at most \(r-1\) vanishing at all \(r\)
distinct \(a_i\), \(i\le r\), so its polynomial coefficients
vanish; the last column then kills the remaining \(b\)-coefficient.
Set \(B=A^{-T}B_0\), where the rows of \(B_0\) are
\(e_i-e_1\), \(2\le i\le r+1\). Use \(B\) as the lower
rows of the slot matrix and write \(\eta=(\det A)^{-1}\).

Put \(S=\sum_{i\le r}x_i\), \(Z=\sum_{i\le r}a_i x_i\),
\(w=x_{r+1}\), and \(s=S+w\). The literal minors give
\[
D=\eta s,\quad y_i=\eta(sa_i-Z),\qquad
z_i=-\eta w\ (i\le r),\quad z_{r+1}=\eta S.
\tag{SE.6}
\]
These formulas also follow from \(B\mathbf1=0\),
\(Ba=e_r\), \(Bb=e_{r-1}\), and their adjugate pairings; the
first-column cofactor fixes exactly the scalar \(\eta\).

Define
\[
Q(s,z)=\prod_{i\le r}(z-a_i s)=(z-2s)^r+s^r,
\qquad Q_i=Q/(z-a_i s).
\]
Substitute (SE.6) in (SE.2). Since \(r\) is odd, the result is
\[
F=-\eta^{r^2+1}sZ^{r-2}
\left(wS^2Q(s,Z)^{r-1}
 +Zw^2Q(s,Z)^{r-2}\sum_{i\le r}x_iQ_i(s,Z)\right).
\tag{SE.7}
\]
For the signs, \(\prod_{i\le r}(sa_i-z)=(-1)^rQ\), while
the last \(y\)-cofactor is \(-\eta Z\). The terms in the sum
\(\mathcal S\) from first \(r\) columns use \(z_i^2=\eta^2w^2\),
and its last term uses \(z_{r+1}^2=\eta^2S^2\). This gives
both terms and the minus sign in (SE.7).

## 2. Both terms of the actual polarization coefficient

The required coefficient is
\([x_1^r\cdots x_r^r w^2]F\). Extract \(w^2\) in (SE.7)
first. The first term differentiates its factor \(sQ^{r-1}\)
once, and the second is evaluated at \(s=S\).
For binary forms use
\(\langle P,R\rangle_N=P(-\partial_z,\partial_s)R|_0\).
Coefficient extraction in the first \(r\) variables is
\((r!)^{-r}\prod_i(\partial_s+a_i\partial_z)^r\).
Its polynomial symbol is \(Q^r\).

Multiplication of the second argument by \(s^2\) transfers to
\(\partial_z^2\) on the first argument, by the Leibniz rule.
Its \(\partial_s\) transfers to multiplication by \(z\).
In the second term of (SE.7), each factor \(x_i\) instead
replaces its corresponding differential power by
\(r(\partial_s+a_i\partial_z)^{r-1}\). Consequently the exact
coefficient is
\[
-\frac{\eta^{r^2+1}}{(r!)^r}
\left(A+rB\right),
\tag{SE.8}
\]
where, with \(N=r^2-1\),
\[
A=\langle z\,\partial_z^2(Q^r),\ s z^{r-2}Q^{r-1}\rangle_N,
\quad
B=\sum_i\langle Q^{r-1}Q_i,\ s z^{r-1}Q^{r-2}Q_i\rangle_N.
\tag{SE.9}
\]
Each pair of arguments has degree \(N\); these identities retain
both contributions to the coefficient.

Translate \(z\mapsto z-2s\) in the actual apolar pairing.
Then \(Q\) becomes \(Q_0=z^r+s^r\), \(z\) becomes \(z+2s\),
and \(\partial_z\) is unchanged. Moreover
\[
Q_i\longmapsto q_i=
\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}\zeta_i^t s^t z^{r-1-t}.
\tag{SE.10}
\]
The root sum is \(\sum_i\zeta_i^h=r\) at \(h=0\),
\(-r\) at \(h=r\), and zero for all other
\(0\le h\le2r-2\). This fixes the whole sum of pairings in
\(B\) without selecting or approximating individual roots.

## 3. Evaluation of the first term

Set
\[
D_i=\binom ri^2(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!,\qquad
U_r=\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i(r-2i)D_i.
\tag{SE.11}
\]
Matching the extra exponents modulo \(r\) in the translated first
pairing allows exactly two terms. The result is
\[
\frac{A}{2^{r-2}}=
\sum_{i=1}^r(-1)^i\binom ri\binom{r-1}{r-i}
(ri)!\,[r(r-i)]!
\left((r-2)(r^2+1)+1-r(r-1)i\right).
\tag{SE.12}
\]
To see the two terms explicitly, the extra \(z\)-degree in the
first argument is zero or one, and the extra \(z\)-degree in
the second is its complement to one. The second derivative gives
\((ri)(ri-1)\). The two remaining factorials are respectively
\((ri-2)!,[r(r-i)+1]!\) and
\((ri-1)!,[r(r-i)]!\). Simplification gives exactly (SE.12).

Use \(\binom{r-1}{r-i}=(i/r)\binom ri\), include the zero
\(i=0\) term, and pair \(i\) with \(r-i\).
Here \(D_{r-i}=D_i\) and \((-1)^{r-i}=-(-1)^i\).
For the quadratic
\(g(i)=(i/r)((r-2)(r^2+1)+1-r(r-1)i)\),
\[
g(i)-g(r-i)=\frac{r^2-r+1}{r}(r-2i).
\]
It follows that
\[
\boxed{A=2^{r-2}\frac{r^2-r+1}{2r}\,U_r.}
\tag{SE.13}
\]

## 4. Exact telescoping of the second term

After the translation, exponent matching forces the extra
\(z\)-degree in \((z+2s)^{r-1}\) to be one. Its coefficient
is \((r-1)2^{r-2}\). The root sum (SE.10) then gives
\[
B=r(r-1)2^{r-2}\beta_r,
\tag{SE.14}
\]
with the following explicit integer sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_r={}&\sum_{v=0}^{r-2}
\binom{r-1}v\binom{r-2}{r-2-v}
(-1)^{rv+r-1}(rv+r-1)!(N-rv-r+1)!\\
&-\sum_{v=1}^{r-1}
\binom{r-1}v\binom{r-2}{r-1-v}
\sum_{p=rv}^{rv+r-2}(-1)^p p!(N-p)!.
\end{aligned}
\tag{SE.15}
\]
The first line uses the root powers \(0,0\). The second uses
the powers \(t,r-t\), \(1\le t\le r-1\), with their
root-sum minus sign. This explains every endpoint and sign.

For \(f(p)=(-1)^p p!(N-p)!\), define
\(g(p)=(-1)^p(p+1)!(N-p)!\). Direct cancellation gives
\[
g(p)-g(p-1)=(N+2)f(p).
\tag{SE.16}
\]
Use (SE.16) on each interval in (SE.15). Set
\(C= r(2r^2-r+1)-1\) and \(T=2r^2-r\).
Combining the endpoint factorials gives exactly
\[
\beta_r=
\frac{\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^{i-1}D_i\,i(C-Ti)}
{(r^2+1)r^3(r-1)}.
\tag{SE.17}
\]
Here is a direct check of the binomial combination, including the
endpoints. The three coefficients at the factorial
\((ri)![r(r-i)]!\), before the common denominator, use
\[
\begin{aligned}
\binom{r-1}{i-1}\binom{r-2}{i-1}
 &=\frac{i^2(r-i)}{r^2(r-1)}\binom ri^2,\\
\binom{r-1}{i-1}\binom{r-2}{i-2}
 &=\frac{i^2(i-1)}{r^2(r-1)}\binom ri^2,\\
\binom{r-1}i\binom{r-2}{i-1}
 &=\frac{i(r-i)^2}{r^2(r-1)}\binom ri^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{SE.18}
\]
Their numerator becomes
\(i((r-i)(2r^2-r+1)+i-1)=i(C-Ti)\), as in (SE.17).
Terms outside the original ranges are zero in these displayed
polynomial expressions, so this combination includes \(i=0,r\).

Finally \(C-Tr=r-1\). Antisymmetrizing the quadratic
\(i(C-Ti)\) under \(i\mapsto r-i\) therefore gives
\[
\boxed{\beta_r=\frac{U_r}{2r^3(r^2+1)},\qquad
rB=2^{r-2}\frac{r-1}{2r(r^2+1)}\,U_r.}
\tag{SE.19}
\]
All manipulations are finite exact factorial identities.

## 5. Nonvanishing and the canonical conclusion

The endpoints \(i=0,r\) in (SE.11) contribute
\(2r(r^2)!\). For every interior index,
\[
\frac{D_i}{(r^2)!}
=\frac{\binom ri^2}{\binom{r^2}{ri}}
\le{\binom ri}^{2-r}\le r^{2-r}.
\tag{SE.20}
\]
The first inequality selects degree \(i\) from every factor of
\(((1+z)^r)^r\). The total absolute interior contribution is
at most \((r-1)(r-2)r^{2-r}(r^2)!<r(r^2)!\), because
\(r^{2-r}\le1/r\) and \((r-1)(r-2)<r^2\).
Thus \(U_r>0\) for every odd \(r\ge3\), including the endpoint.

Adding (SE.13) and (SE.19), the exact coefficient (SE.8) is
\[
\boxed{-\frac{\eta^{r^2+1}2^{r-2}}{(r!)^r}
\frac{r(r^2-r+2)}{2(r^2+1)}\,U_r\ne0.}
\tag{SE.21}
\]
It detects the actual retained-slot/common-polarization map.
The lower-map parameter check (SE.4), the exact annihilator
inclusion, and the multiplicity-one complementary-column pairing
prove R-029. Field extension to the displayed root splitting field
and inclusion into larger ambient spaces commute with all of these
maps, just as in ES.18.

The primary lower-map input is Sra, *The q-Foulkes problem III:
On Foulkes' conjecture with a graded inner factor*, Theorem 1.3,
[primary PDF](https://suvrit.github.io/papers/qfoulkes3/qfoulkes3-v1.pdf).
The exact kernel map is K.16–K.22 and P.9–P.16, and the highest
polynomial and complement maps are BS.8–BS.15. The scalar reduction
in this report is an exact evaluated family, without a historical
novelty claim.


# The full second-cofactor strip below the square bound

## R-030. Statement

For all integers
\[
r\ge2,\qquad 1\le j\le r-1,\qquad r+j\text{ odd},
\tag{CS.1}
\]
put
\[
a=r+1,\quad b=r^2-r+j,\quad H=r^2+j,
\qquad
\lambda=(H,(H-1)^{r-2},H-3,j+1).
\tag{CS.2}
\]
The normalized canonical map
\(h_{b,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^b\operatorname{Sym}^aV
\to\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^bV\)
has target and image multiplicity exactly one at \(\lambda\),
in every dimension where this Schur functor is nonzero.

The first endpoint \(j=1\) is in R-027 and the odd-\(r\)
endpoint \(j=2\) is R-029. The proof below establishes the full
range (CS.1), including the critical degree \(b=r^2-1\) at
\(j=r-1\). No historical novelty claim is made.

## 1. Actual polynomial, complement, and lower canonical map

Retain the determinant \(D\), last two cofactor rows \(y,z\)
and polynomial \(\mathcal S\) defined in (SE.2). The highest
polynomial is
\[
F=D^{j-1}\mathcal S\prod_i y_i^{r-2}=F_{r+1,H,r}.
\tag{CS.3}
\]
The exponent is nonnegative. The literal raising substitutions and
column-permutation calculation BS.8–BS.9 give precisely the slot
degree \(b\), the row weights (CS.2), and slot symmetry, since
\(H\) is odd. The complementary-column perfect pairing and
primitive Young projectors BS.10–BS.15 identify its multiplicity
with the unique highest wedge (SE.3). Hence the target multiplicity
is one; this includes \(r=2\), where that complement is \((3,3)\).

The exact retained-slot/common-polarization annihilator inclusion
K.16–K.22 applies because
\[
b-r=(r-1)^2+j-1\ge(r-1)^2.
\tag{CS.4}
\]
The lower canonical map is surjective by Sra's Theorem 1.3.
Thus a nonzero value of
\((T_{r,r,b}\otimes1)\delta F\) proves the actual image
multiplicity. We compute its coefficient
\([x_1^r\cdots x_r^r w^j]F\), with the first \(r\) first-row
bases zero and the retained slot's first-row coordinate equal to
\(w\). Its total first-row degree is exactly \(H\).

## 2. Literal matrix and both coefficient terms

Use exactly the matrix (SE.5): \(a_i=2+\zeta_i\),
\(\zeta_i^r=-1\), \(a_{r+1}=0\); \(b_i=0\) for
\(i\le r\), \(b_{r+1}=1\); reference column 1; rows
\((a_i^e-a_1^e)\), \(2\le e\le r-1\), then \(b_i\),
then \(a_i-a_1\). Its inverse-transpose construction and
Vandermonde proof remain valid at \(r=2\), with the first row
list empty. Put \(\eta=(\det A)^{-1}\),
\(S=\sum_{i\le r}x_i\), \(Z=\sum_{i\le r}a_ix_i\), and
\(s=S+w\). The actual cofactors are (SE.6).

Set \(Q=(z-2s)^r+s^r\) and \(Q_i=Q/(z-a_i s)\).
Multiplying those cofactors gives the polynomial identity
\[
F=(-1)^{r-2}\eta^{H-1}s^{j-1}Z^{r-2}
\left(wS^2Q(s,Z)^{r-1}
 +Zw^2Q(s,Z)^{r-2}\sum_i x_iQ_i(s,Z)\right).
\tag{CS.5}
\]
This is (SE.7) with its determinant power and general parity
retained. It keeps the contribution from every summand of
\(\mathcal S\).

Put \(N=r^2+j-3\). The Leibniz and apolar adjoint calculations
of (SE.8)–(SE.10) give the exact coefficient
\[
\frac{(-1)^{r-2}\eta^{H-1}}{(j-1)!(r!)^r}
\left(A_j+r(j-1)B_j\right),
\tag{CS.6}
\]
where, after the determinant-one translation and with
\(Q_0=z^r+s^r\),
\[
A_j=\left\langle (z+2s)^{j-1}\partial_z^2(Q_0^r),
 s^{j-1}(z+2s)^{r-2}Q_0^{r-1}\right\rangle_N,
\tag{CS.7}
\]
\[
B_j=\sum_i\left\langle (z+2s)^{j-2}Q_0^{r-1}q_i,
 s^{j-1}(z+2s)^{r-1}Q_0^{r-2}q_i\right\rangle_N
\quad(j\ge2),
\tag{CS.8}
\]
and \(B_1=0\). Here
\(q_i=\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}\zeta_i^t s^t z^{r-1-t}\).
In particular \(\sum_i\zeta_i^{t+u}\) is \(r\) at zero,
\(-r\) at \(r\), and zero otherwise in this range.
The normalization in (CS.6) comes from the two derivatives of
\(w\)-orders \(j-1,j-2\) and from differentiating each
\(x_i\) in the second term: the latter gives the factor \(r\).

## 3. Two finite integer sums

Define \(f_N(p)=(-1)^p p!(N-p)!\). The parity condition makes
\(N\) even, so this is also the apolar sign in terms of the
\(z\)-degree. Exact exponent matching modulo \(r\) in (CS.7)
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal A={}&\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}
\binom ri\binom{r-1}{r-i}
\binom{j-1}\ell\binom{r-2}{j-1-\ell}\,
(ri)(ri-1)f_N(ri-2+\ell),\\
A_j={}&2^{r-2}\mathcal A.
\end{aligned}
\tag{CS.9}
\]
For \(j\ge2\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B={}&\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-2}
\binom{j-2}\ell\binom{r-1}{j-1-\ell}
\Bigg[
\sum_{v=0}^{r-2}\binom{r-1}v\binom{r-2}{r-2-v}
 f_N(rv+r-1+\ell)\\
&\hspace{16mm}-
\sum_{v=1}^{r-1}\binom{r-1}v\binom{r-2}{r-1-v}
\sum_{t=1}^{r-1}f_N(rv+r-1-t+\ell)
\Bigg],\\
B_j={}&r\,2^{r-2}\mathcal B.
\end{aligned}
\tag{CS.10}
\]
Put \(\mathcal B=0\) at \(j=1\). To check these ranges,
the extra exponents in (CS.7) sum to \(j-1\). In (CS.8)
they also sum to \(j-1\), while the two root exponents sum
either to zero or to \(r\). Their largest possible extra sum
is \(j+r-3\), so no other congruence class representative is
possible. The two root sums give the two signed terms in
(CS.10). All powers of 2 are exactly \(2^{r-2}\).

Thus it suffices to prove the unconditional strict inequality
\[
\boxed{\mathcal A+r^2(j-1)\mathcal B>0.}
\tag{CS.11}
\]
We prove it by explicit bounds for \(r\ge10\), and give the
complete finite integer certificate for \(2\le r\le9\).

## 4. Endpoint and interior bounds for the first sum

Write \(M_0=r^2(r^2-1)N!\). The absolute terms of
\(\mathcal A\) at \(i=r\) strictly increase with \(\ell\).
Indeed their consecutive ratio is
\[
\frac{(j-1-\ell)(r^2-1+\ell)}
{(\ell+1)(r-j+\ell)}
\ge\frac{N}{(j-1)(r-2)}>1
\quad(\ell<j-1).
\tag{CS.12}
\]
The last term is positive, because its exponent is \(N\),
which is even. Pairing backwards gives the endpoint contribution
at least
\[
M_0\left(1-\frac{(j-1)(r-2)}{N}\right)
\ge M_0\frac{5r-8}{r^2+r-4}
\ge M_0\frac3r.
\tag{CS.13}
\]
At \(j=1\) the endpoint is exactly \(M_0\). The last
inequality follows from \((r-4)(2r-3)\ge0\), and the middle
one uses the maximum permitted \(j=r-1\).

For every \(1\le i\le r-1\), binomial convolution gives
\[
\binom N{ri-2+\ell}
\ge\binom{r^2-2}{ri-2}\binom{j-1}\ell,
\quad
\binom{r^2-2}{ri-2}
=\frac{ri(ri-1)}{r^2(r^2-1)}\binom{r^2}{ri}.
\tag{CS.14}
\]
The derivative factor in (CS.9) cancels against this exact
binomial ratio. Use
\(\binom{r^2}{ri}\ge\binom ri^r\),
\(\binom{r-1}{r-i}\le\binom ri\),
\(\binom ri\ge r\), and sum the remaining binomial in
\(\ell\). The total absolute interior contribution, divided
by \(M_0\), is at most
\[
(r-1)2^{r-2}r^{2-r}<\frac1{r^2}\qquad(r\ge10).
\tag{CS.15}
\]
For the strict bound, write it as
\((r-1)r^2(2/r)^r/4\). Since \(r\ge10\), it is at most
\(64/r^5<1/r^2\), by replacing the exponent \(r\) by 8
and using \(r-1<r\).

## 5. An absolute bound for the second sum

Assume \(j\ge2\); the term is zero at \(j=1\).
First separate the endpoint \(v=r-1\) in the second line of
(CS.10). Put \(h=j-1-\ell\), so \(1\le h\le j-1\).
Its absolute value divided by \(N!\) is at most
\[
\sum_{h=1}^{j-1}\binom{j-2}{h-1}\binom{r-1}h
\sum_{t=1}^{r-1}\binom N{t+h-1}^{-1}.
\tag{CS.16}
\]
In this range \(t+h-1\le2r-4\), and the consecutive ratios
of the reciprocal binomial coefficients are at most
\[
\frac{2r-3}{N-2r+4}\le\frac2{r-1}.
\]
The inner sum in (CS.16) is therefore at most
\((r-1)/(r-3)\) times \(\binom Nh^{-1}\).
Set \(\tau=(r-1)/N<1/(r-1)\). Termwise comparison of
falling factorials gives
\(\binom{r-1}h/\binom Nh\le\tau^h\).
Summing now bounds (CS.16) by
\[
\frac{r-1}{r-3}\tau(1+\tau)^{j-2}
<\frac6{r-1}.
\tag{CS.17}
\]
Here \((1+1/(r-1))^{r-1}<3\): expand by binomials, bound
the coefficient of degree \(q\) by \(1/q!\), and bound
the sum for \(q\ge2\) by \(\sum_{q\ge2}2^{1-q}=1\),
strictly at some terms. Also \((r-1)/(r-3)\le2\).

All remaining terms have the following elementary bound. Put
\(M=r^2-1\). Binomial convolution yields
\[
\binom N{p_0+\ell}\ge\binom M{p_0}\binom{j-2}\ell.
\tag{CS.18}
\]
It cancels the first binomial in the outer sum of (CS.10);
the sum of the second binomial is at most \(2^{r-1}\).
For its first inner sum, put \(i=v+1\), so \(1\le i\le r-1\).
The exact ratio is
\[
\frac{\binom{r-1}{i-1}\binom{r-2}{i-1}}
{\binom M{ri-1}}
=\frac{i(r-i)}{r(r-1)}
\frac{\binom ri^2}{\binom{r^2}{ri}}
\le r^{2-r}.
\tag{CS.19}
\]

For the second inner sum, now \(1\le v\le r-2\) and
\(rv\le p_0\le r(v+1)-2\). A binomial row is unimodal,
because its consecutive ratio \((M-p)/(p+1)\) decreases with
\(p\); so its minimum on this interval is at an endpoint. At those
endpoints, the exact adjacent-factor formulas give
\[
\binom M{rv}\ge r^{-2}\binom{r^2}{rv},\qquad
\binom M{r(v+1)-2}\ge r^{-2}\binom{r^2}{r(v+1)}.
\tag{CS.20}
\]
For the second inequality, put \(q=r(v+1)\); its ratio is
\(q(q-1)/(r^2(r^2-q+1))\ge r^{-2}\), since \(q\ge2r\).
Let \(C_v=\binom rv\). The numerator weight satisfies
\[
\binom{r-1}v\binom{r-2}{v-1}
\le C_vC_{v+1}\le r\min(C_v,C_{v+1})^2.
\]
The first inequality follows from including the chosen subsets
in sets of sizes \(r\), and the second from the adjacent
binomial ratio, which lies between \(1/r\) and \(r\).
Using \(\binom{r^2}{ri}\ge C_i^r\) and
\(C_i\ge r\) in (CS.20) consequently bounds each such
weight/denominator ratio by \(r^{5-r}\).

There are \(r-1\) terms of the first kind and
\((r-2)(r-1)\) of the second. Their combined bound, divided by
\(N!\), is therefore
\[
2^{r-1}\bigl((r-1)r^{2-r}
 +(r-2)(r-1)r^{5-r}\bigr)<\frac{513}{r^3}
\quad(r\ge10).
\tag{CS.21}
\]
For a direct numerical-free check, replace \((2/r)^r\) by
\((2/r)^{10}\). The two terms are then at most
\(512/r^7<1/r^3\) and \(512/r^3\), respectively.
Combining (CS.17),(CS.21), and
\(6/(r-1)\le20/(3r)\), gives
\[
\frac{|\mathcal B|}{N!}
<\frac{20}{3r}+\frac{513}{r^3}
\le\frac{3539}{300r}<\frac{12}{r}.
\tag{CS.22}
\]
Since \((j-1)/(r^2-1)<1/r\), this proves
\[
\frac{|r^2(j-1)\mathcal B|}{M_0}<\frac{12}{r^2}.
\tag{CS.23}
\]
Together (CS.13),(CS.15),(CS.23) imply
\[
\frac{\mathcal A+r^2(j-1)\mathcal B}{M_0}
>\frac3r-\frac{13}{r^2}>0\qquad(r\ge10).
\tag{CS.24}
\]

## 6. Exhaustive smaller parameters and the exact conclusion

There are exactly twenty pairs in (CS.1) with \(2\le r\le9\).
Their full exact positive integers are recorded in the table appended
below, generated from the displayed finite sums (CS.9),(CS.10).
For each pair, the companion program also expands the two complete
binary pairings (CS.7),(CS.8) separately and checks equality with
those sums. Thus this finite step is a reproducible exact integer
certificate, with all parameter pairs and values supplied.

Equations (CS.6),(CS.9),(CS.10) give the literal coefficient
\[
\boxed{
\frac{(-1)^{r-2}\eta^{H-1}2^{r-2}}{(j-1)!(r!)^r}
\left(\mathcal A+r^2(j-1)\mathcal B\right)\ne0.}
\tag{CS.25}
\]
The uniform bound and the exhaustive finite certificate prove its
nonvanishing for every stated parameter. The highest multiplicity
pairing, exact annihilator map and lower-map range (CS.4) then
prove R-030. All constructions commute with characteristic-zero

All additional maps and scalar factors are the actual cofactor,
Young-projector, retained-slot and apolar morphisms proved above.
